subject: Computing

unit.unitOverview:
There are two big ideas, and both are simple. The first is knowing when the internet is here or not. Our devices show us little pictures called icons that tell us whether we are connected. When the internet is here to use, we say it is available; when it is not here, it is not available.

The second big idea is sharing safely. When devices are connected, information can travel between them — something on one device can be seen on another. That is wonderful: we can send a photo or a warm hello to family far away, from Hargeisa to Mogadishu in a moment. But because other people can see what we send, we learn to think first. They finish with five simple stay-safe rules.

outcomes: Know when a network and the internet are available (here to use) and when they are not available.
Read simple icons that show a device is connected without wires, connected with a wire, or not connected at all.
Say what you cannot do with no internet — send emails, look at websites, or watch online videos.
Understand that connected devices share information, so something on one device can be seen by another.
Understand, in a gentle way, that malware is a program that is bad for a computer, and that we do not open files from people we do not know.

concepts.title: Is the internet here? (network availability)
concepts.explanation:
Sometimes the internet is here for us to use, and sometimes it is not. Our devices tell us with little pictures called icons. When the internet is here, we say it is available. When it is not here, it is not available. With no internet, we cannot send emails, look at websites, or watch online videos.

Our devices can join a network with a wire, or through the air with no wire. But how do we KNOW if we are joined and the internet is working?
concepts.example: Full lines mean we are joined through the air. Now the internet is not available.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you name one thing you cannot do with no internet?

concepts.title: Sharing across a network (think before you share)
concepts.explanation:
When devices are connected, they can share information. That means something on one device can be seen by another device. Sharing is wonderful — but because other people can see what we send, we learn to think first.

Pass the slips around the circle, hand to hand. Could the person next to you see your paper? Could lots of people see it as it went around?
concepts.example: Do the passing game from the textbook. Give you a slip of paper to write or draw something small and happy on (a star, a fruit).
concepts.checkYourself: Can you name one lovely thing about sharing?

concepts.title: Keep your private things private (personal information)
concepts.explanation:
Personal information is private information about YOU. It includes your home address, your phone number, your family's names, your birthday, and your school's name. The biggest risk on a network is sharing personal information, because people we do not know might see it.

On one: “My favourite colour is green.” On the other: “My home is at.” Ask: “Which one is fine to tell everyone? Which one is private, just for our family?” Explain warmly: “Personal information is like the key to your house.
concepts.example: You would not hand your house key to someone you do not know. We keep personal information private in the same way.”
concepts.checkYourself: Can you name two things that are personal and private?

concepts.title: Careful what we open (malware)
concepts.explanation:
Malware is a program that is bad for a computer. Some people try to trick us by sending malware across a network. We receive information when we open a website or download a file — so we do not open files, messages or links from people we do not know. A computer with malware acts strangely: it slows down, strange adverts pop up, files will not open, or it stops working.

The word malware means bad software — a naughty program. It can make a computer poorly, a bit like a germ makes us poorly. How do we stay well?
concepts.example: We are careful. A computer stays well when we are careful too — we only open files and messages from people we know and trust, and we check with a grown-up.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you know not to open files from people you do not know?

concepts.title: Our safety rules (staying safe and being kind)
concepts.explanation:
We finish by gathering everything into five simple stay-safe rules. Teachers may know these as the SMART rules. Introduce each rule with a simple phrase and, if you like, an action. Say them warmly, not as warnings.

Try it: This session leads straight into the.
concepts.example: Find one real example of our safety rules (staying safe and being kind) around you, or on a device you use. Say out loud what it is and why it fits.

esafety.title: Keep personal information private
esafety.text: Your full name, address, school, phone number, birthday and passwords are personal information. Never type them into a game, an app or a website, and never send them to someone you only know online.

esafety.title: Check before you trust
esafety.text: Anyone can put anything on the internet, so not everything you read is true. Check an important fact on a second, different website, and ask an adult you trust if you are not sure.

esafety.title: Tell someone if something worries you
esafety.text: If anything online upsets you, or someone asks you for personal information or to keep a secret, stop, leave the page and tell an adult you trust straight away. It is never your fault.

esafety.title: Respect other people's work
esafety.text: Pictures, music and writing belong to whoever made them. Use work that is free to use, and say where you got it. Your own work belongs to you — put your name on it.

reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer:
Malware is a program that is bad for a computer. Some people try to trick us by sending malware across a network. We receive information when we open a website or download a file — so we do not open files, messages or links from people we do not know. A computer with malware acts strangely: it slows down, strange adverts pop up, files will not open, or it stops working.

The word malware means bad software — a naughty program. It can make a computer poorly, a bit like a germ makes us poorly. How do we stay well?
